chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from 'Amr ibn 'Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Shu'ayb, from Abu Ja'far al-Madaini, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
A generous youth, burdened with sins, is more beloved to Allah than a worshipping stingy old man.

key_terms.عَابِدٍ: Worshipper, one engaged in acts of devotion

ai.seo_question: Why is a generous sinner considered more beloved to God than a stingy worshipper?
ai.summary: In Shia scholarship, this hadith from al-Kafi is often interpreted not as a contradiction to piety, but as a comparative evaluation of character traits, suggesting that the active virtue of generosity (sakhā') in a young, sin-prone individual is more beloved to Allah than the static piety of a miserly elder. Scholars note that 'murraqqa' (burdened by sins) does not imply the generous person is worse than the devout one, but rather that the specific quality of open-handedness carries greater weight in this specific context than the lack thereof in the ascetic. This highlights the practical importance of social generosity and overcoming stinginess as key markers of spiritual vitality.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziiyad, from Amro Bin Usman, from Muhammad Bin Shuayb, from Abu Ja’far Al Madainy, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘A youth drenched in the sins is more Beloved to Allah<sup>azwj</sup> than a worshipping stingy old man’.
en.sarwar: 14. A number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Amr ibn ‘Uthman from Muhammad ibn Shu’ayb from abu Ja’far al- Mada’iniy who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said that
a young generous man excessively involved in sins is more beloved to Allah than an old worshipping man who is stingy.”
